source_text: Omnia apostoli secundum deum utique docuerunt, omnia evangelii revolverunt. Ubi illos ostendis praeceptum fugiendi de civitate in civitatem restaurasse? quia nec potuissent tale quid constituere tam contrarium exemplis suis, ut fugam mandarent, qui cummaxime de vinculis vel insulis, quibus ob confessionem, non ob fugam nominis continebantur, ad ecclesias scribebant. Infirmos sustinere iubet Paulus, utique enim non fugientes. Quomodo enim sustineantur absentes? An patientia? Dicit sustinendos, sicubi per infirmitatem fidei suae offenderint, sicut pusillanimes consolari, non tamen in fugam mitti. Sed cum admonet, ne locum malo demus, non fugae suggerit consilium, sed iracundiae docet temperamentum, et si redimendum tempus dicit, quia dies nequam sunt, non per fugam, per sapientiam conversationis lucrari nos vult commeatum. Ceterum qui lucere nos iubet velut filios lucis non iubet fuga abscondi ut filios tenebrarum. Stare immobiles praecipit, utique nec fuga mobiles, et accinctos, in fugam, an in occursum evangelii? Arma quoque demonstrat, quae fugituris non essent necessaria. Inter quae et clypeum, quo possitis tela diaboli extinguere, resistentes sine dubio et excipientes omnem vim illius. Proinde et Iohannes pro fratribus quoque animas ponendas docet, nedum pro domino. Hoc a fugientibus non potest adimpleri. Denique memor Apocalypsis suae, in qua timidorum exitum audierat, de suo sensu admonet et ipse timorem reiciendum: Timor, inquit, non est in dilectione. Sed enim perfecta dilectio foras mittit timorem, quia timor suppliciamentum habet, utique ignem stagni; qui autem timet, non est perfectus in dilectione, dei scilicet. Porro quis fugiet persecutionem, nisi qui timebit? Quis timebit, nisi qui non amavit? Spiritum vero si consulas, quid magis sermone illo spiritus probat? Namque omnes paene ad martyrium exhortatur, non ad fugam; ut et illius commemoremur: Publicaris, inquit, bonum tibi est; qui enim non publicatur in hominibus, publicatur in domino. Ne confundaris, iustitia te producit in medium. Quid confunderis laudem ferens? Potestas fit, cum conspiceris ab hominibus. Sic et alibi: Nolite in lectulis nec in aborsibus et febribus mollibus optare exire, sed in martyriis, uti glorificetur qui est passus pro vobis.
thought_title: Apostolic teaching and the Spirit forbid flight
orientation: Tertullian is arguing from the apostles' own teaching and from the Spirit's sayings that flight from persecution was never commanded for Christians.
pass_a_gloss: The apostles taught all things according to God, to be sure; they unrolled all things of the gospel. Where do you show that they restored the command of fleeing from city to city? Because they could not have established such a thing, so contrary to their own examples, so as to command flight, who, especially from chains or islands, in which they were held because of confession, not because of flight from the name, were writing to the churches. Paul commands to support the weak, to be sure, not those fleeing. For how are the absent supported? Or by patience? He says they are to be supported, if anywhere through weakness of their faith they have stumbled, just as the faint-hearted are to be comforted, not however to be sent into flight. But when he warns that we should not give place to evil, he does not suggest the counsel of flight, but he teaches the moderation of anger, and if he says that time is to be bought back, because the days are evil, he wants us to gain a reprieve not through flight, but through wisdom of conduct. Moreover, he who commands us to shine like sons of light does not command us to be hidden by flight like sons of darkness. He commands us to stand immovable, to be sure, and not movable by flight, and to be girded—for flight, or for the encounter of the gospel? He also points out weapons, which would not be necessary for those about to flee. Among which also the shield, by which you may extinguish the darts of the devil, resisting without doubt and receiving all his force. Therefore John also teaches that lives are to be laid down even for brothers, much less for the Lord. This cannot be fulfilled by those fleeing. Finally, mindful of his Revelation, in which he had heard the end of the cowardly, he warns from his own mind that fear itself is to be cast out: Fear, he says, is not in love. But perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment, to be sure the fire of the pool; but he who fears is not perfect in love, namely of God. Furthermore, who will flee persecution, except he who will fear? Who will fear, except he who has not loved? But if you consult the Spirit, what does he approve more by that saying of the Spirit? For he exhorts nearly all to martyrdom, not to flight; so that we may also remember that saying: You are publicly exposed, he says, it is good for you; for he who is not publicly exposed among men, is publicly exposed in the Lord. Do not be ashamed; righteousness brings you into the middle. Why are you ashamed while bearing praise? Power comes to be, when you are seen by men. So also elsewhere: Do not choose to go out in beds, nor in miscarriages and soft fevers, but in martyrdoms, so that he who suffered for you may be glorified.

lemmas.gloss: you are publicly exposed, made public

choices.why: The verb literally means to unroll a scroll, suggesting full exposition of the gospel; 'unrolled' preserves the physical image and the sense of complete teaching.
Tertullian asks where the apostles renewed or reinstated the command to flee; 'restored' captures the idea of bringing back an earlier command.
The verb means to bear up or hold up, matching the pastoral sense of supporting the weak; 'support' is the natural English equivalent.
The compound means small-souled or faint-hearted; 'faint-hearted' preserves the literal sense and the contrast with courage.
The noun means a leave of absence or passage; in context it means gaining time or relief from evil days, so 'reprieve' fits the sense of buying back time.
The verb means to be made public or exposed before men; 'publicly exposed' captures the sense of being brought into the open as a witness.

pass_b_english: The apostles certainly taught everything according to God, and unfolded the whole gospel. Where do you show that they restored the command to flee from city to city? They could not have established anything so contrary to their own examples. While they were held in chains or on islands because of their confession, not because of flight from the name, they wrote to the churches.

Paul commands us to support the weak (1 Thessalonians 5:14), and certainly not those who are fleeing. How can the absent be supported? Or is it by patience? He says they are to be supported if they have stumbled through weakness of faith, just as the faint-hearted are to be comforted, but not sent into flight. And when he warns us not to give place to the devil (Ephesians 4:27), he is not suggesting the counsel of flight; he is teaching moderation of anger. And when he says to buy back the time, because the days are evil (Ephesians 5:16), he wants us to gain a reprieve not through flight but through wisdom of conduct.

Besides, the one who commands us to shine as children of light (Ephesians 5:8) does not command us to hide ourselves in flight like children of darkness. He instructs us to stand immovable (Ephesians 6:14), certainly not to be moved by flight, and to be girded. For flight, or for the encounter of the gospel? He also points to weapons that would not be necessary for those about to flee. Among them is the shield, with which you can extinguish the darts of the devil (Ephesians 6:16), resisting without doubt and receiving every assault of his.

So John also teaches that lives are to be laid down for brothers (1 John 3:16), much more for the Lord. This cannot be fulfilled by those who flee. Finally, mindful of his Revelation, in which he had heard the end of the cowardly (Revelation 21:8), he himself warns from his own understanding that fear must be cast out. "Fear," he says, "is not in love. But perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment" (1 John 4:18), certainly the fire of the lake. "Whoever fears is not perfected in love," that is, in the love of God.

But who will flee persecution except the one who fears? Who will fear except the one who has not loved? And if you consult the Spirit, what does that saying of the Spirit prove more than anything? For it exhorts almost everyone to martyrdom, not to flight. Let us remember that saying of the Spirit too: "You are publicly exposed," it says; "it is good for you. For whoever is not made public among men is made public in the Lord. Do not be ashamed; righteousness brings you into the open. Why are you ashamed while bearing praise? Power comes when you are seen by men." So also elsewhere: "Do not wish to depart in beds, or in miscarriages and soft fevers, but in martyrdoms, so that the one who suffered for you may be glorified."
